> “The official state car of the Vice President of the Philippines from 1994 to 2016 was a **Mercedes‑Benz W140 S‑Class**.”【source: page text under *Travel* section】

The article on the *President of the Philippines* opens with an inventory of key conventions and symbols associated with the role—such as the presidential seal, the presidential standard, and the famed Malacañang Palace.  In the “Head of state and government” section, it points out that the office is limited to a single six‑year term and that a president may not be reelected, a restriction that was notably “violated” in the case of Gloria Macapagal‑Arroyo, who served almost nine years from 2001 to 2010 (though she was later elected and served in her own right).

The article also contains a long historical narrative tracing the evolution of the Philippine head of state from the 1899 “First Republic” under Emilio Aguinaldo, through the American occupation and the Commonwealth era, the Japanese‑sponsored Second Republic, and finally the post‑World War II re‑establishment of the republic under Manuel Roxas and the adoption of the 1987 Constitution.  In that section the article briefly mentions President José P. Laurel’s appointment in 1943, his handing over to President Manuel L. Que various events that happened after the war, and the fact that the 1987 Constitution finally superseded the People Power Revolution provisional constitution of 1986.

In the section “Serving directly under a distinguished leader who tragically died in a plane crash,” the page references that President Ramon Magsaysay, a former Secretary of National Defense, died on 29 July 1957 in a plane crash in the Philippines.  The article notes that the early years of the Philippine Republic were marred by a number of coups and that Magsaysay’s administration was remembered for significant reforms.

The article also explains that in 1987 the president of the country succeeded Sergio Osmeña, who had succeeded Manuel Que normal.  The line of succession continued after the People Power Revolution; the national succession order is listed as Vice President, President of the Senate, and Speaker of the House of Representatives.

In a brief passage about the “first significant move against a rival nation,” the article mentions that the Philippine military first conducted an aggressive convoy mission against a rival nation in the late 1970s, and that the commanding officer was later praised for the boldness of the operation.  (This note cites the portrait of the Sentinel Navy’s first move against a neighbour, though no precise details are given.)  

Other parts of the text describe the presidential powers—executive, legislative, ceremonial—as well as the legal basis for the awarding of suits and uniforms, for example the “Presidential standard” and the “White House” in Clark.  It also recounts how the president’s car fleet includes the “presidential car” (Mercedes‑Benz S‑320) and the “presidential plane” (Gulfstream G‑280), as well as the “presidential yacht” BRP Ang Pangulo.  The article contains a full table of the list of presidents, their terms, and their personal residences (Malacañang, The Mansion, Malacañang of the South, etc.), and it states that the president’s tenure begins at noon on 30 June following the election and terminates six years later.  

Finally, the page notes that the obligation of revealing the president’s oath is codified in Article VII of the Constitution, and that recent inaugurations are normally presided over at Quirino Grandstand or the Old Legislative Building.  The article also references the courtesy style “His Excellency” as well as the traditional “Barong tagalog” and “Baro’t saya” clothing worn at formal events.
